digest.intro: Surveillance infrastructure, AI sovereignty, and mythology that traveled further than anyone knew.

items.title: Pax Silica — The US Government's Named Framework for AI as Foreign Policy
items.blurb: The State Department has given a name and a doctrine to what was previously implicit: 'Pax Silica' is the US framework for treating compute, critical minerals, and AI supply chains as the geopolitical equivalent of 20th-century oil and steel. Declaration signatories commit to aligned AI infrastructure — meaning non-signatories are, by design, outside the consensus. Worth reading as a primary source because the framing is unusually candid about what's actually being organized.

items.title: Mistral Raises €3B — Sovereign Open-Weight AI to the Frontier
items.blurb: The largest equity raise in European tech history positions Mistral explicitly against the Pax Silica logic: their pitch is that governments and enterprises shouldn't have to surrender 'control over the infrastructure and intelligence loop' to a US-aligned provider. Samsung led the round, joined by EQT's Scaleup Europe Fund. Read alongside the State Department piece above, and the geopolitics of AI concentration comes into unusually sharp relief.

items.title: DHS 'Predictive Policing' Units Are Analyzing Americans' Financial Habits — Then Pulling Them Over
items.blurb: Border Patrol's Predictive Intelligence Targeting Teams (PITT) analyze financial behavior and feed intelligence to local police, who then execute stops under pretextual violations — in one case, an 'obstructed license plate' in Montana after the system flagged a man's financial activity. The CDT's framing is precise: 'genuine probable cause cannot be synthetically generated,' and when the underlying model is secret, there's no meaningful way to challenge a stop. This is parallel construction industrialized.

items.title: There's a New 'Google Jail' for Independent Wikis
items.blurb: Since a March 2024 algorithm change, roughly 90% of wikis launching on brand-new domains show up in Google Search for only their main page — catastrophic for knowledge communities whose traffic is almost entirely search-driven on article pages. The practical result is that independent wikis migrating off Fandom (which is covered in auto-playing video ads) can't escape into the open web without effectively disappearing. One infrastructure player's ranking logic is quietly deciding which community knowledge projects are viable.

items.title: LibreOffice Breaks Download Records After Declaring It Has No AI Features
items.blurb: LibreOffice 26.8 hit over a million downloads in its first week — a record — after The Document Foundation explicitly stated it won't ship generative AI by default until the technology meets six principles including zero telemetry, no content leaving the device without authorization, and no single-vendor dependency. The foundation's framing: 'Yes, no AI is now a feature.' Absence of a capability becoming the product signal is worth tracking.

sections.heading: Science at the edge of translation

items.title: WeatherNext 3 — DeepMind's Hourly Global Forecast Model, Landing as NOAA Gets Defunded
items.blurb: DeepMind's third-generation weather model generates hourly forecasts by drawing directly from raw satellite imagery rather than preprocessed data, hitting 5km resolution on surface temperature and humidity — significantly more accurate than prior models even in locations not seen during training. The timing is the real story: this capability is expanding precisely as public forecasting infrastructure in the US is being gutted. Private AI weather capability and defunded public meteorology are now on diverging trajectories.

items.title: The Two Christian Saints Who Are Secretly the Buddha
items.blurb: Saints Barlaam and Josaphat — venerated in both Catholic and Orthodox calendars — are a direct structural retelling of the Buddha's life story, transmitted via a Persian intermediary ('Bodisav' from 'Bodhisattva'), then into Arabic as 'Budhasaf', then into Georgian as the Balavariani in the 10th century, and finally absorbed into Christian hagiography so completely that the origin was invisible for centuries. The name 'Josaphat' is a phonetic corruption of 'Bodhisattva.' This is not influence or borrowing — it is wholesale identity laundering across three civilizations.

facts.fact: The name 'Josaphat' — a Christian saint venerated since the 10th century — is a phonetic corruption of the Sanskrit word 'Bodhisattva,' meaning the Buddha before enlightenment.
Rubbing hands with soil, peat, and moss for just 20 seconds measurably increases skin microbial diversity even after rinsing with tap water, according to Finnish Environment Institute research.
Roughly 90% of wikis that have launched on brand-new domains since March 2024 show up in Google Search only for their main page — making community migration off Fandom effectively a disappearing act.
Mistral's €3B Series D is the largest equity fundraising round ever completed by a European technology company, three years after the company's founding.

Border Patrol's PITT units have been operating secretly long enough that the Associated Press was already investigating their license plate reader use last year — the financial analysis layer revealed by 404 Media is an undisclosed addition on top.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A masterwork of essay cinema that treats memory, ritual, and image-making as interlocking systems — Marker moves between Guinea-Bissau and Tokyo asking how cultures encode meaning into objects, ceremonies, and screens. It makes you want to rethink every image you've ever made.

art_picks.title: Vera Molnár — Drawings & Prints
art_picks.creator: Vera Molnár
art_picks.why: The grandmother of generative art went unreasonably deep for decades on a single question: what is the minimum deviation from order that produces feeling? Her rule-based plotter drawings look alive precisely because of their controlled drift — a direct ancestor of the WebGL work you're making.

art_picks.title: Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill
art_picks.creator: Grouper
art_picks.why: Liz Harris makes music that sits exactly at the edge where physical texture and digital blur become indistinguishable — vocals buried in tape hiss, guitar dissolving into reverb clouds. Handmade and structurally radical at the same time.

events.name: Camille Henrot: Dogs
events.venue: Doris C. Freedman Plaza, Central Park (5th Ave & 60th St)
events.why: Henrot's first public sculpture show in NYC uses the dog — that most domesticated, status-coded, emotionally loaded symbol — as a lens on what humans outsource to animals; handcrafted delight with anthropological weight, free and outdoors.

events.name: Sarah Michelson: nowhere
events.venue: MoMA, Marron Family Atrium, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Michelson colonizes MoMA's atrium as a daily working studio — performance folded into exhibition form, bodies navigating institutional space in real time, no separation between rehearsal and show; the museum becomes the medium.

events.name: Brice Marden: I Am Plane Image
events.why: First comprehensive Marden survey in New York in twenty years — six decades of encaustic and oil paintings that obsess over the line between surface and depth, drawing on calligraphy, mythology, and Greek landscape; rare chance to see the full arc in one room.

events.name: Affordable Art Fair NYC
events.why: With the Armory Show pushed to the 24th, most galleries front-loaded their fall openings to align with this window — the Affordable Art Fair becomes a useful sweep of what the mid-tier gallery scene is actually betting on this season.
